faq.a: The liver makes more transferrin to capture any available iron, raising the binding capacity.
faq.q: Why is TIBC high in iron deficiency?

faq.a: Early deficiency may show normal TIBC; combine with ferritin and clinical picture.
faq.q: Can TIBC be normal in iron deficiency?

faq.a: Use transferrin concentration (if available) or calculate saturation from serum iron and estimated transferrin; clinical judgment becomes paramount.
faq.q: What if the lab cannot measure TIBC?

exam: A 30‑year‑old woman with heavy menstrual bleeding and low hemoglobin: which iron study best distinguishes iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease? — Explain TIBC’s role and expected pattern.
A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with anemia; ferritin is 300 µg/L. How do you interpret TIBC? — High TIBC points to iron deficiency despite high ferritin.
In a malaria‑endemic area, a child has anemia and elevated ferritin. What additional test helps you decide if iron supplementation is safe? — Check TIBC; low/normal suggests ACD, high suggests IDA.

You receive a TIBC of 180 µg/dL in a malnourished adult with anemia. What does this indicate and what is your next step? — Low TIBC suggests protein‑energy malnutrition or chronic inflammation; assess nutritional status and treat underlying cause.

During a blood transfusion reaction work‑up, serum iron is 250 µg/dL and TIBC is 300 µg/dL. What does the transferrin saturation tell you? — Saturation ≈ 83 %, indicating iron overload, not typical for transfusion reaction; consider hemolysis.

A patient with chronic hepatitis B has a TIBC of 220 µg/dL. How does liver disease affect interpretation? — Liver dysfunction reduces transferrin synthesis, lowering TIBC and potentially masking iron deficiency.
You suspect sideroblastic anemia in a farmer exposed to pesticides. Which iron study pattern supports this diagnosis? — Normal/low TIBC with high serum iron and high ferritin.

In a resource‑limited clinic, only serum iron is available. How can you still differentiate IDA from ACD? — Combine iron level with clinical clues (diet, infection) and, if possible, a rough estimate of transferrin using total protein.
ai.title: Total Iron Binding Capacity
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: TIBC measures the blood's capacity to bind iron, reflecting transferrin levels. It helps differentiate iron deficiency from anemia of chronic disease, especially where ferritin is unreliable.

b: High TIBC → low iron stores; Low TIBC → inflammation or malnutrition
sections.p: TIBC is an indirect measurement of serum transferrin, the main iron‑transport protein. It is calculated from serum iron and transferrin saturation and is reported in µg/dL.
Transferrin synthesis occurs in the liver and rises when iron is scarce, falling during inflammation (acute‑phase response). TIBC therefore mirrors iron availability and hepatic synthetic function.

b: IDA: high TIBC, low serum iron, low ferritin (if not inflamed)
ACD: low/normal TIBC, low serum iron, normal‑high ferritin
sections.p: In low‑resource settings, ferritin may be elevated by infection, making TIBC essential for diagnosing iron‑deficiency anemia (IDA) versus anemia of chronic disease (ACD).

t.b: What is the amount of circulating iron? Low values suggest deficiency or sequestration.
What proportion of binding sites are occupied? <20 % supports IDA; 20‑50 % is typical.
What are iron stores? Elevated in inflammation, may mask IDA.

b: Ask about hookworm exposure – common cause of iron loss in East Africa.
Check for hepatomegaly or jaundice – may indicate chronic liver disease affecting transferrin.
sections.p: When faced with anemia, always ask about diet, chronic infection (TB, HIV, malaria), gastrointestinal loss, and pregnancy. Look for pallor, tachycardia, and signs of chronic disease.

b: Low TIBC can be seen in protein‑energy malnutrition, not just ACD.
Acute hemolysis raises serum iron but does not change TIBC.
sections.p: Relying on ferritin alone in infection, misinterpreting a normal TIBC as normal iron status, and forgetting that severe malnutrition lowers transferrin production.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe anemia with heart failure signs (e.g., orthopnea, tachycardia >120 bpm)
Rapid drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL in 24 h
Unexplained jaundice with anemia suggesting hemolysis
